title: Repentance and Salvation in Jewish Thought
hook: What if repentance and salvation were never about escaping hellfire at all?
tldr: In the Hebrew Scriptures and Jewish thought, repentance means returning to God as a community, and salvation means deliverance and blessing in this life. Gehinnom is mostly a temporary place of purification, not eternal damnation. Tying repentance to escaping endless torment is a later Christian development.
big_idea: Repentance restores relationship; it is not a ticket out of hell.

points.title: Repentance was communal, not individual
points.text: Most biblical calls to repent use a plural you, addressed to Israel as a nation, promising restored land, peace and blessing rather than individual escape from damnation.

points.title: T'shuva means turning back
points.text: The Hebrew word for repent literally means return or turn. Its aim is restoring and strengthening a loving relationship with God and neighbor, not avoiding eternal torment.

points.title: Metanoeo means change your mind
points.text: The Greek word for repentance basically means to change one's mind. In the Gospels it was a national call for Israel to change its ways, with national calamity as the warning.

points.title: Salvation means deliverance here and now
points.text: In Scripture and in Jewish usage today, salvation means rescue, protection, victory, a longed-for child or success after hardship, not escape from a torturous afterlife.

points.title: Gehinnom purifies and is temporary
points.text: Rabbinic literature describes Gehinnom as a temporary place where souls are purified before Gan Eden, with the Talmud setting a maximum of one year.

points.title: Test every theology by fatherhood
points.text: No good father kills a child or disowns them for failing to repent. Yet many Christians picture God doing exactly that, which breeds anxiety rather than peace.

sections.summary: The first part of the book explores the linguistic roots and historical context of hell, drawing on early and later Christian traditions and Jewish interpretations. It examines the etymology of the word and how pagan, Jewish and Christian lenses saw hell, surveying its development across cultures, eras and religious frameworks.

sections.h: Repentance tied to hell in some traditions
sections.summary: Calvinism, Evangelicalism, Pentecostalism, Messianic Judaism and others link repentance directly to hell, as when John MacArthur warns those rejecting the gospel of forever with demons. In Jewish thought T'shuva matters greatly but is not linked to salvation or hellfire. It is about restoring and enhancing a relationship built on love, trust and respect, not fear, and avoiding legalism and judgmentalism.

Biblical repentance is not a one-time mystical event but a change of view about God, often turning from idols, and doing justice for the oppressed, fatherless and widow. The Mosaic Law was a practical guide to ethical living. Sin threatened social harmony, so repentance meant restitution, like returning stolen property. Sin and repentance are mainly horizontal and communal, hence loving our neighbor.

Our individualistic world shaped Christianity, but the Torah sees the individual as part of the community, and English hides whether you is plural. The Hebrew word for repent means return or turn. Ezekiel calls for collective transformation; Jeremiah promises staying in the land; Joel seeks national repentance to avert disaster; Chronicles promises healing the land; Zechariah addresses post-exile rebuilding; Hosea exposes national unfaithfulness.

The Hebrew Scriptures present repentance as a collective concept. Its outcome was restored communal unity, peace, prosperity, and blessing on Israel's land and offspring. The focus was a healthy, loving relationship as a nation under God, shaping the quality of life here and now.

T'shuva is restorative and relational, not fear-driven. A good father never threatens to kill his children, and God never threatened Israel so, though sin had severe consequences. Deuteronomy 28 promises prosperity, fertility and protection for obedience, and famine, disease and defeat for disobedience. Charles Dyer notes both are temporal; the worst was physical death. Any repent-or-burn warning meant earthly consequence.

Nothing changed in the New Testament. A Second Temple Jew heard repentance as the return of God's blessing, end of exile and restored kingdom. Metanoeo means change the mind, like switching from vanilla to chocolate. For Israel it meant following Jesus's Way of loving enemies, compassion, generosity, justice and care for the poor, not Pharisaic traditions. For the nations, it meant leaving idols for Israel's God.

sections.h: A national call, a national calamity
sections.summary: John the Baptist's plural call to repent was to Israel; reading it as accepting Christ as Savior is anachronism, since Jesus had not yet emerged or been crucified. Jesus took up the same message. Failure to repent meant national calamity: unless you repent you will perish means Jerusalem's destruction in 70-135 with the temple and exile, not burning in hell.

When Jesus called individuals to repent, it was about relationships, not accepting an atonement that had not yet happened. Luke 17:3 says rebuke a sinning brother and forgive if he repents, with no threat of burning forever. Luke 15's Lost Sheep, Lost Coin and Prodigal Son picture restoring a strained relationship, not rescue from eternal punishment for rejecting Christ.

Faith alone is a placebo in most Western theology. Arminians say you are justified by faith but lose salvation if you fail to live holy and endure, ending in endless torment. Calvinists say once saved, always saved, but failure shows you were never saved. Arminianism adds works at the start, Calvinism retrospectively; both tie salvation from hellfire to works, much like some Catholic theology.

sections.h: Works matter, but not for escaping fire
sections.summary: Works are vital for the quality of our lives and others', and for rewards and roles in the afterlife. Paul, a Jew, knew where faith and works divide, and that his rewards depended on how he lived. Rewards can be earned or lost, but if rescue from a cosmic incinerator must be earned or sustained, no one could have peace.

sections.h: What if our Father were Calvinist or Arminian?
sections.summary: Jesus taught us to see God as an unconditionally loving Father. A child's sin damages the relationship, but a parent never stops being their parent, never burns them. A wayward student who drinks and skips church would not provoke thoughts like I must kill them (Arminianism) or they were never mine (Calvinism). Yet many anxious Christians believe God sees them this way.

sections.h: The Corinthians and a fearful faith
sections.summary: God's children sin like anyone. Paul called the Corinthians sanctified yet rebuked their sins, motivating them by God's fatherly love, never threats of torture. Endless salvation debates suggest an absence of inner peace and insecurity, faith tied to anxiety, God seen as an oppressive tyrant. In Judaism deeds shape life, rewards and status in the hereafter, but almost never eternal fate.

For Jews, salvation means God's blessings and redemption in this life: conceiving a child after difficulty, business success after hardship, victory in conflict. Scripture agrees: deliverance from Egypt, the Lord as light and stronghold, rescue from the wicked, strength and defense, and return from exile with peace and security. Salvation concerns earthly realities, not escape from a torturous afterlife.

sections.h: Hell in Judaism: a present reality
sections.summary: Jewish afterlife views are varied and not explicit. Gan Eden and Gehinnom differ from Christian heaven and hell; 2 Maccabees laid groundwork for posthumous reward and punishment. Hell is mostly a reality on earth: the Holocaust's six million murdered Jews, and October 7th, 2023, with rape and babies burned by Hamas. Israeli billboards read Release them from Hell now; it brought hell to both sides.

Judaism holds many views, but the prevalent one sees Gehinnom as a temporary place of purification before Gan Eden. Talmud Rosh Hashanah 17a sets the maximum stay at one year, after which the cleansed soul ascends. Berachot 5a says suffering in this world can atone, a hell on earth. Mishnah Eduyot 2:10 says the purified go to Gan Eden; only the truly wicked are annihilated.

Rabbi Manis Friedman says hell is the repair of damage, not revenge: burning off the bad to salvage the good, a painful readjustment as the soul leaves the body. Only those headed to heaven go through it, keeping their identity, memories and relationships. Someone like Hitler, with nothing to salvage, loses identity and becomes generic energy. Other rabbis think even Hitler may retain God's image.

Like Christianity's Westboro Baptist Church, Judaism has a few marginalized rabbis, mostly Sephardic from Muslim countries, who absorbed Islamic hellfire ideas and consign almost everyone to eternal torment; they are not mainstream. Jewish and Christian views of hell differ partly because their views of sin, atonement, salvation and repentance differ.

mythfact.myth: Biblical calls to repent were individual appeals to avoid hell.
mythfact.fact: Most were plural, national calls to Israel, promising restored land, peace and blessing, or warning of earthly calamity.

mythfact.myth: Unless you repent you will perish means burning in hell.
mythfact.fact: It warned Israel of national destruction, fulfilled in Jerusalem's fall, the temple's destruction and exile in 70-135.

mythfact.myth: Judaism teaches eternal damnation in Gehinnom.
mythfact.fact: The prevalent Jewish view sees Gehinnom as temporary purification, at most one year per the Talmud, before Gan Eden.

mythfact.myth: Faith alone settles salvation in Protestant theology.
mythfact.fact: Arminians and Calvinists both tie salvation from hellfire to works, one at the outset and one retrospectively.

quotes.text: Both the blessing and the judgment in view here are temporal, not eternal. The [most severe] judgment was physical death, not eternal damnation.
You see, the concept of hell is "the repair of damage." Hell is not simply revenge on God's part. It's repair.
God is love, not a narcissistic, sadistic psychopath.

verses.role: Plural call to repent within a passage on Israel's collective accountability.
National repentance leads God to forgive and heal the land.
Blessings for returning to God are earthly: prosperity, fertility, protection.
Curses for not repenting are temporal: famine, disease, defeat.
John's plural call to Israel, not an invitation to accept Christ as Savior.

Repentance as interpersonal reconciliation between brothers.
Parables of the lost depict restored relationship, not escape from eternal punishment.
Salvation as deliverance from physical danger and oppression.
Paul knew his afterlife rewards, not salvation, depended on how he lived.

quiz.q: What does the Hebrew word for repent literally mean?
quiz.why: The Hebrew word for repent or repentance literally means return or turn.

quiz.q: According to Talmud Rosh Hashanah 17a, what is the maximum stay in Gehinnom?
quiz.why: It states the maximum duration of punishment is one year, after which the cleansed soul ascends to paradise.

quiz.q: In Luke 13:3, what does perish refer to?
quiz.why: It warned Israel of national destruction: the temple, Jerusalem and exile in 70-135.
